top10_for_owner_review.task_text: Analyze road segment geometry. The script analyzes the geometric characteristics of road segments by computing curvature radius, turning angle, and orientation (clockwise/counterclockwise/straight) for every three consecutive vertices along input line geometries. It groups consecutive vertices with identical orientation into unified segments, classifies each segment as 'curve' or 'tangent' based on a user-defined radius threshold (default 2000 m), and outputs a vector layer with attributes: segment_id, type (curve/tangent), orientation, mean radius, and mean angle per aggregated segment. Simplification (Douglas-Peucker, snap-to-grid, or Visvalingam) is optionally applied pre-analysis to reduce vertex noise.

Snap line vertices to points. The script snaps specified vertices (start, end, or mid-vertices) of line geometries in a source vector layer to the nearest point from a points layer, optionally constrained by attribute-based conditions (e.g., field comparisons using operators like '=', '!=', 'contains') and maximum snapping distance. It supports advanced matching logic (AND/OR/XOR combinations of two conditions), configurable reuse of points (once per layer/feature/part), spatial indexing for efficiency, reprojection if CRS mismatched, and multipoint-to-singlepoint conversion. Output is a new vector layer with modified geometries preserving original attributes.

Map canopy vegetation extent and height. The script maps the spatial extent of canopy vegetation (LiDAR classification class 5) over Grigny, France, by merging and filtering four LAS point cloud files to retain only ground-filtered vegetation points, rasterizing them at 1 m resolution, vectorizing the resulting binary presence raster into polygons, repairing geometries, and computing zonal mean height statistics against a normalized Digital Surface Model (nDSM); outputs include a 1-m vegetation presence raster, a shapefile of vegetation polygons with area attributes, and a statistics-enhanced shapefile with weighted-mean canopy height (in meters), min/max heights, and total vegetated surface area (m²/km²).

Calculate maximum distance to water. The script calculates, for each paddock polygon, the maximum Euclidean distance from any location within that paddock to the nearest water point. It does so by: (1) harmonizing coordinate reference systems between paddock and water point layers; (2) for each paddock, extracting only the water points that intersect it; (3) rasterizing those water points into a binary raster (value 1 at water locations); (4) computing a GDAL proximity raster (distance in map units to nearest pixel with value 1); and (5) clipping the proximity raster to the paddock boundary. The output is a set of clipped proximity rasters — one per paddock containing at least one water point — saved as GeoTIFF files named after the paddock (e.g., 'PaddockA.tif'), where pixel values represent distance in the CRS units (e.g., meters). No aggregation or summary statistics (e.g., max value extraction) is performed beyond raster generation; the rasters themselves are the final outputs.

Compute median DSM within grid zones. The script computes the median value of a Digital Surface Model (DSM) raster, masked by a binary mask layer, within each polygon feature of a grid vector layer. The workflow includes: (1) retrieving three local QGIS layers named 'dsm', 'mask', and 'grid'; (2) multiplying the DSM raster (band 1) with the mask raster (band 1) using GDAL Raster Calculator to produce a masked DSM; (3) computing zonal statistics (median only) of the masked DSM over the grid polygons using QGIS Zonal Statistics; (4) replacing null median values in the resulting 'med_median' attribute field of the grid layer with 0. No external remote sensing data sources, time-series, or cloud-based processing are involved — all inputs are preloaded local layers in the QGIS project. Study area, time range, satellite/sensor, and coordinate reference system are not specified.

Identify disconnected network segments. The script analyzes topological connectivity of a line-based river or transport network layer relative to an initial 'River Mouth' point/geometry. It iteratively selects connected line segments by vertex proximity and spatial adjacency, starting from the River Mouth, using dissolve-by-ID, vertex extraction, selection-by-location, and iterative expansion until no new features are selected. It outputs two vector layers: (1) 'Excerpt Disconnected' — line segments with no topological path to the River Mouth (i.e., isolated branches), and (2) 'Connected section' — line segments reachable via shared vertices/intersections from the River Mouth, representing the topologically continuous upstream/downstream network.

Estimate floodwater depth. The script estimates water depth across a flooded area by generating a triangulated irregular network (TIN) surface from elevation-sampled points along the flood boundary, smoothing the TIN, subtracting it from a clipped high-resolution DEM (MERIT 90m), and masking/clipping the resulting depth raster to the original flood polygon while enforcing non-negative values. Outputs include a final depth raster ('depth_final.sdat') representing estimated inundation depth in meters.

Extract upstream catchment polygons. The script processes a river network vector layer and a point sites layer to extract, fix, and dissolve upstream catchment polygons for each site based on the RSC_NUMNA (lower Strahler order) and RSC_UNUMNA (upper Strahler order) attributes. It filters river segments within the Strahler order range associated with each site, repairs geometries, dissolves the resulting segments into a single polygon per site, and outputs a feature layer where each feature is a dissolved upstream catchment polygon attributed with the site’s code field value.

Filter structures near rivers. The script filters and relocates point structures (e.g., bridges, culverts) from MTMD and road–river intersections to produce a cleaned point layer of infrastructure features within 100 m of the hydrographic network. It does so by: (1) computing line intersections between river and road networks; (2) merging those intersections with MTMD point structures; (3) buffering merged points by 2 m; (4) dissolving overlapping buffers; (5) computing centroids of dissolved buffers to aggregate nearby features; (6) extracting only those centroids within 100 m of the river network; and (7) assigning a unique integer ID ('fid') to each resulting point. The output is a vector point layer named 'New_structure' containing filtered, aggregated, and uniquely identified infrastructure points proximal to rivers.

Calculate satellite visibility C-index. The script computes the radar-based C-index raster (ranging from -1 to +1) that quantifies the geometric sensitivity of satellite SAR (e.g., Sentinel-1) line-of-sight (LOS) measurements to ground movement along terrain slope direction. It derives this index using DTM-derived slope and aspect, plus user-provided satellite acquisition geometry (incidence angle θ and track/azimuth angle φ) to compute directional cosines (H, N, E). The workflow includes: (1) generating constant rasters for θ and φ; (2) computing azimuth-corrected φ (φ+90); (3) calculating H = cos(θ), N = cos(π/2−θ)·cos(π−φ), E = cos(π/2−θ)·cos(3π/2−φ); (4) extracting slope and aspect from the input DTM; (5) evaluating the full C-index formula: C = N·cos(S)·sin(A−π/2) + E·(−1)·cos(S)·cos(A−π/2) + H·sin(S); (6) converting C to absolute percentage (|C|×100); and (7) reclassifying the percentage into five ordinal visibility classes (0–20%, 20–40%, ..., 80–100%). Outputs are three co-registered rasters: C_index (unitless, −1 to +1), Percentage_c_index (0–100%), and Class_of_visibility (integers 1–5).
